An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
Smashed every gauge in the cockpit
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette KressByKali Hays, Technology reporter and Osmond Chia, Business reporterPublished17 November 2026Updated 27 minutes ago
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.

item.description:
Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous people in Brazil raises concerns over safety
A rare encounter with isolated Awa Indigenous people in Brazil’s Amazon has raised concerns about their safety and the growing threats to their forest territoryBySTEVEN GRATTAN Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 7:01 PM
Share
BOGOTA, Colombia -- A rare encounter between Indigenous people living in isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest and members of a neighboring community has prompted government protections amid concerns about the group’s health and threats to its forest home.
The encounter began Monday near a government access control post and the Guajajara Indigenous village of Tawari in the northeastern state of Maranhao, according to a statement Tuesday from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples.
The ministry said around 20 members of the isolated Awa people had been sighted approaching the area in the Arariboia Indigenous Territory, but cautioned that information remained preliminary as authorities assessed the situation. The encounter has raised concerns about why members of a group that has spent decades hunting, fishing and gathering food while avoiding outsiders would suddenly approach a neighboring community, particularly as illegal logging, hunting and other intrusions threaten their forest territory. Images of the encounter have also drawn widespread attention.
Sarah Shenker, head of Survival Brasil, part of Survival International, an organization that advocates for Indigenous peoples’ rights, called the encounter “a crisis moment really and a wake-up call,” urging Brazilian authorities to crack down on illegal intrusions into Awa territory.
She said the images could help reinforce the existence of isolated Indigenous groups, whose presence is sometimes disputed by those seeking access to their lands. But she warned that the circumstances surrounding the encounter were troubling.

item.title: [BBC China] As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura BickerChina correspondentPublished2 hours ago
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something...

item.title: [CBS News World] Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
item.description:
An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in Middle East conflicts.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."

item.description:

Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia Ireland, Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya Abishev, BBC News RussianPublished17 November 2026
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.

item.description:
Latest

David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
Reporting from Manila
Here’s the latest.
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “trade deal” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.

Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
The Catholic cardinal who oversees care of the faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem to convey Pope Leo XIV's presence during troubled times for ChristiansByGIOVANNA DELL'ORTO Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:29 PM
JERUSALEM -- The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.
Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.
“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”
Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.
Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.
Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.
“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”
Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that killed nine worshippers during a service at a Greek Orthodox church.

item.title: [ABC News World] Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
item.description:
Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in CzechoslovakiaByThe Associated PressNovember 17, 2026, 1:50 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BRATISLAVA, Slovakia -- People in Slovakia took to the streets Tuesday to rally against the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that brought an end to decades of communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
Opposition parties organized the protests in dozens of communities across the country, where Fico remains as Europe’s most pro-Russian leader since Hungary’s Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We’ve had enough of Fico,” chanted people in Bratislava, where organizers estimated 25,000 gathered in the downtown SNP square. One banner had a message for the prime minister: “Go to hell.”
The capital's rally united the liberal groups Progressive Slovakia and the Democrats with pro-business Freedom and Solidarity, the conservative Christian Democrats and an alliance of ethnic Hungarians. Together they hope to defeat Fico and his coalition government in next year’s parliamentary election.

Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByLaura Gozzi, Ilya Abishev, BBC Russian Defence Correspondent and Richard Irvine-Brown, BBC VerifyPublished17 November 2026
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.
A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.
How did the seven-stage operation play out?
The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.
For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished17 November 2026
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

View image in fullscreen
The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters
Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.
Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.
